props.text: Not a general dentist with a weekend course. A board-certified prosthodontist who has spent a career rebuilding what other people gave up on.
You have probably been told this is complicated. That it will take years, cost a fortune, or simply cannot be done.
Usually that is a verdict on the tools available to whoever was looking, not on your mouth.
Most implant failures are not surgical failures. They are planning failures, and planning is the discipline a prosthodontist trains three extra years to do.
One of twelve recognized dental specialties.
Why patients travel to see Dr. Nahlah.
Most implant cases pass through three or four sets of hands. Here, they don’t.
Board-certified prosthodontist with three years of specialist training beyond dental school.
A weekend implant course, or a referral out.
Surgery and final teeth planned and placed by the same specialist.
Handed between a surgeon, a dentist and an outside lab.
The final smile is designed first, then implants are placed to serve it.
Implants placed first, restoration figured out afterwards.
Complex and failed cases accepted, including work other practices decline.
Nitrous oxide or oral sedation in the chair, so a full-arch case is done in one sitting.
Local anesthetic, or a referral for sedation.
Thin-arch (FP1) full arches wherever the bone allows: teeth, not a slab of pink acrylic.
One thick FP3 prosthesis, whatever the case looks like.
A digital laboratory inside both offices, so shade and fit are corrected while you wait.
Posted to an outside lab, and waited on for weeks.
Every implant placed through a computer-generated surgical guide.
Placed freehand, judged by eye on the day.

A cone-beam scan shows the bone we actually have to work with. You leave knowing whether you are a candidate, what it costs, and how long it takes.
The final teeth are designed before a single implant is placed. You approve the result in advance rather than hoping for it.
Implants are placed through a surgical guide built from your scan, under sedation if you want it. Many patients leave the same day with fixed teeth.
Once healing is complete the definitive teeth go in, shaped, shaded and bite-balanced by the same specialist who planned them.
Four things you will not find down the road.
Planning, surgery, sedation and the lab that makes your teeth, all in the same building, run by the same team. These four are what that actually buys you.
A digital laboratory in both practices.
McLean and Alexandria each have their own lab and their own technician. Shade, shape and fit are corrected in minutes rather than posted to a third party and waited on for weeks.
Placed to a plan, not by eye.
A cone-beam scan maps the bone, the positions are planned in software, and a printed surgical guide puts every implant at the planned angle and depth.
Veneer preparations are kept as thin as the case allows, so what is already yours stays yours.
Teeth, not a slab of acrylic.
Where the bone allows it, a full arch is restored as FP1: crowns on implants, with no bulky pink base. The difference is below.
FP1, FP2, FP3, and why we plan for the first.

Every full-arch implant prosthesis is one of three types. What separates them is how much of it is teeth, and how much is pink acrylic standing in for gum and bone. Most practices fit one kind. Here the arch is planned as thin as the case will carry.
No added pink, no extra bulk
Typically on more natural gum architecture
The pink that is added still follows the natural gum contour
Rarely indicated, and often not ideal
Thick pink acrylic stands in for gum and bone
Typically best where there is bone loss, and a lower hygiene risk
The same arch, three ways. The pink is the difference.
A thin arch is not always possible. Where bone loss is advanced, FP3 is both the honest answer and the stronger one. What is worth asking is whether anyone planned for the alternative.
How a full arch is planned
